REPOS.name: LibreChat
REPOS.blurb: A ChatGPT-style chat interface you run yourself, with many model providers behind one login.
REPOS.what: LibreChat is an open-source chat front-end that recreates the ChatGPT experience — conversations, model switching, presets, multi-user accounts — but running on your own machine or server. Behind the one interface you can plug in OpenAI, Claude, Google, local models and more, and switch between them per conversation.
REPOS.who: Anyone who wants one chat interface for several AI providers, or a private chat set-up for a small team without per-seat subscriptions.
REPOS.cost: The software is free. Talking to it is not: each model provider bills its own API usage per token. Connect a local model instead and the cost becomes your hardware and electricity.
steps: Install Docker first
Everything LibreChat needs — the app, its database, its search service — ships as containers, so Docker Desktop (or Docker Engine on Linux) is the only real prerequisite.
docker --version
Clone the repo
One command pulls the whole project onto your machine.

git clone https://github.com/danny-avila/LibreChat.git
cd LibreChat
Create your config file
LibreChat ships an example settings file. Your real one is a copy of it — this is the file every later change happens in.
cp .env.example .env
Add at least one model key
Open .env in any text editor and paste in a key for at least one provider. No key, no answers — the interface runs, but there is no brain behind it yet.

OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...        # inside .env
# or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, GOOGLE_KEY, etc.
Start the stack
Docker downloads the images and starts the app plus its database and search containers in the background. The first start takes a few minutes.
docker compose up -d
Open it and create the first account
Visit http://localhost:3080 in your browser and sign up. The first account created becomes the admin.
REPOS.watch: "Free to install" is not "free to run". Every message rides on your own API keys, and if you host it on a rented server, that server bills by the month too.

REPOS.name: Vibe-Trading
REPOS.blurb: An AI agent from HKUDS that researches markets for you: pulls price data, reads the news, writes up the analysis.
REPOS.what: Vibe-Trading is a research agent built by HKUDS (the University of Hong Kong's data science lab). You ask a question in plain language — a ticker, a sector, a theme — and the agent plans its own research: fetching market data, scanning news and filings with its tools, then writing a structured note of what it found.
REPOS.who: Developers learning how agents work on a real problem, and traders who want a tireless research assistant — not a signal bot that tells them what to buy.
REPOS.cost: The code is free. The thinking is not: the agent runs on a large language model API that you pay for per token, and deeper data sources may need their own (sometimes paid) keys.
steps: Clone the repo
Grab the project from the HKUDS GitHub organisation.

git clone https://github.com/HKUDS/Vibe-Trading.git
cd Vibe-Trading
Create a virtual environment
Keeps this project's Python packages separate from everything else on your machine, so versions never fight.

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate    # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
Install the dependencies
Pulls in the data, charting and agent libraries the project needs. Expect a few minutes and a few hundred megabytes.
pip install -r requirements.txt
Configure your keys
Copy the example env file and add your LLM API key — the agent cannot reason without one. Add market-data keys too if your data source needs them.

cp .env.example .env
# then edit .env and add your keys
Launch it and ask a question
Start the agent and give it a research question in plain language. Watch the plan it makes before it spends your tokens — that plan is the product.
python main.py
REPOS.watch: It produces research, not returns. A fluent write-up and a tidy backtest are not financial advice — verify anything it says before real money moves.

REPOS.name: FinceptTerminal
REPOS.blurb: A Bloomberg-style market terminal built by the community: quotes, charts, screeners and news in one dense screen.
REPOS.what: FinceptTerminal recreates the feel of a professional market terminal — watchlists, charts, company financials, screeners, portfolio views — as a free desktop app. Under the hood it pulls from free and public data feeds rather than an institutional data contract, which is both why it exists and where its limits are.

REPOS.cost: Free software running on free data feeds. Some sources ask for a free API key; none of it is institutional-grade, real-time exchange data.
steps: Clone the repo
Standard first step — pull the project down from GitHub.

git clone <the clone URL from the repo's Code button>
cd FinceptTerminal
Create a virtual environment
A desktop app this size pins many library versions; isolate them.

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate    # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
Install the dependencies
This is the slow step — charting and data libraries are heavy. Let it finish.
pip install -r requirements.txt
Add any data keys it asks for
If the README or a .env.example lists data-provider keys, sign up for the free tiers and paste them in. The terminal runs without some of them, with fewer panels alive.
cp .env.example .env   # if the repo ships one
Launch the terminal
Start the app with the run command from the README's quick start, then build a watchlist of tickers you actually follow and explore one panel at a time.

REPOS.name: Open-LLM-VTuber
REPOS.blurb: A voice-driven AI character with a Live2D avatar that talks back — and can run fully offline on your own machine.
REPOS.what: Open-LLM-VTuber wires a full voice pipeline to an animated character: speech recognition hears you, a language model composes the reply, text-to-speech speaks it, and a Live2D avatar moves and lip-syncs along. Every stage is swappable — cloud services if you want easy quality, local models if you want it private and offline.
REPOS.who: Streamers, tinkerers, and anyone who wants a hands-on project that teaches how ASR, LLMs and TTS fit together.
REPOS.cost: Free software. Offline mode trades API bills for your own compute; cloud LLM, voice or speech options bill per use. First run also downloads model files — budget the disk space.
steps: Clone the repo, with its submodules
The project bundles other projects inside it; the extra flag pulls those in too. Skip it and pieces will be missing later.

git clone --recurse-submodules <the clone URL from the repo's Code button>
cd Open-LLM-VTuber
Install the Python dependencies
The README's install path (pip/uv) sets up the server and the voice stack.
pip install -r requirements.txt
Choose your brain and voice

Open the config file (conf.yaml) and pick the LLM backend — a local one via Ollama for offline use, or a cloud API — plus the speech recognition and voice engines. This file is where the project's personality lives too.
Start the server
The backend starts listening and loads the models it needs — the first load is the slow one.
python run_server.py
Open the character and talk
Open the web client the server points you to, allow microphone access, and speak. Expect to return to the config file more than once to tune voices and prompts.
REPOS.watch: The demo videos hide the setup. A voice pipeline has many moving parts — mic, recognition, model, voice, avatar — and your first evening is configuration, not conversation.

REPOS.name: Camofox Browser
REPOS.blurb: A stealth, Firefox-based browser that AI agents drive — handing them compact page snapshots instead of raw HTML soup.
REPOS.what: Agents are bad at the raw web: a modern page is megabytes of HTML, and reading it burns tokens while teaching the model almost nothing. Camofox Browser runs pages in an anti-detection Firefox-based browser and returns a trimmed, structured snapshot of what is actually on the page — the text, the buttons, the links — that an agent can afford to read and act on.
REPOS.who: Agent builders whose bots need to browse real, JavaScript-heavy sites: research assistants, testers, monitoring tools.
REPOS.cost: Free software. The real cost is compute — a genuine browser per session is hundreds of megabytes of RAM — plus your agent's own model bill.
steps: Install it the way the README says
Camofox ships for container or Node-based setups; follow the repo's current quick start rather than any blog post, this area moves fast.
docker compose up -d    # or the npm path from the README
Start the browser server
The service launches the browser engine and waits for instructions over its API.
Point your agent at it
Configure your agent framework's browser tool with Camofox's address, instead of a default headless browser.
Ask for a page, get a snapshot
The agent requests a URL and receives the compact snapshot — readable content and actionable elements, not the page's entire DOM.
Act through the same API
Clicks, typing and navigation are issued as commands against the snapshot's element references, then a fresh snapshot shows the result.
REPOS.watch: Stealth cuts both ways: automate only sites you are allowed to, respect terms of service, and expect serious memory use once sessions run in parallel.

REPOS.name: Hyperframes
REPOS.blurb: By HeyGen. Write a video as HTML and CSS — timed scenes in a web page — and render it into a real MP4 file.
REPOS.what: Hyperframes is HeyGen's open framework for programmatic video. A composition is an HTML document whose elements carry timing; a headless browser plays the page frame by frame while FFmpeg assembles the frames into a finished video. If you can build a web page, you can generate videos — hundreds of them, from data, without opening an editor.
REPOS.who: Developers generating video at scale: ad variants, product explainers, data stories, personalised clips.
REPOS.cost: Free and open source. Rendering spends your CPU/GPU time and disk instead — a long or high-resolution video is real compute, not a quick export.
steps: Install Node.js 18 or newer
Hyperframes is a JavaScript toolchain; Node is the entry ticket. FFmpeg must be available too — the renderer uses it to assemble the video.
node --version
Get the project
Clone the repo, or install the CLI into your own project from npm as the README describes.
git clone <the clone URL from the repo's Code button>
Install dependencies
Pulls in the headless browser and rendering stack — a sizeable download the first time.
npm install
Start from an example composition
Copy a sample scene and change the text, colours and timing. Scenes are just HTML elements with time attributes — your web skills transfer directly.
Render it
The render command plays your composition in a headless browser and writes the finished MP4 to the output folder.
npx hyperframes render
REPOS.watch: It is a renderer, not an editor — there is no timeline to drag clips on, and every font and image must exist locally at render time or the build fails.

REPOS.name: claude-ads
REPOS.blurb: A skill that plugs into Claude Code and audits your Google and Meta ad accounts like a media buyer hunting waste.
REPOS.what: claude-ads is a packaged skill — a bundle of expert instructions and checks — for Anthropic's Claude Code. Point it at your ad account data and it works through an audit: account structure, budget spread, tracking health, search terms and audiences, then reports findings ordered by likely wasted spend.
REPOS.who: Freelance media buyers, and small teams running Google or Meta ads without an agency looking over their shoulder.
REPOS.cost: The skill itself is free. Using it needs Claude Code (a Claude subscription or API usage), and the audit reads data from ad accounts you own or are authorised to manage.
steps: Install Claude Code
The skill runs inside Anthropic's terminal agent, so that goes in first, signed into your Claude account.
Add the skill
Clone the repo into your Claude skills folder (global, or per-project) as its README directs — Claude Code picks skills up from there automatically.
git clone <the clone URL from the repo's Code button>
Prepare your ad data
Export the account data the audit asks for — campaign and search-term reports from Google Ads or Meta — or connect the source the README supports. Recent data; a full quarter beats a good week.
Run the audit
Invoke the skill in Claude Code and let it work through the account. It will ask for files or access as it reaches each check.
Work the findings top-down
The report is ordered by impact: fix tracking and the biggest waste first, and treat every recommendation as a hypothesis to check against your own numbers before pausing anything.

MYREPOS.name: agent-standards
MYREPOS.blurb: Discovers your codebase's real coding conventions from evidence, then feeds only the relevant ones to your AI coding agent.
MYREPOS.what: agent-standards is a lightweight, tool-agnostic system for discovering a codebase's implicit coding conventions, turning them into evidence-backed standards, and injecting only the relevant ones into AI coding agents — Claude Code, Cursor, or anything that reads markdown. It is an independent, MIT-licensed project (inspired by, but not affiliated with, Agent OS), and it labels itself experimental / educational.
MYREPOS.how: It runs a five-stage loop: discover → review → index → inject → score. Deterministic AST miners extract observable patterns — naming, docstrings, annotations, import order, test naming — each with hard evidence (followed/observed counts and sample files); no LLM is required, and an optional local Ollama pass may polish prose but can never touch evidence, ids or approval status. A human approves candidates, BM25-style lexical retrieval then picks the few standards relevant to the current task within a token budget, and standards you mark critical: true can be enforced as CI/pre-commit gates. The system is three layers: a zero-dependency POSIX shell layer (python3 only upgrades it), a Python engine for exact AST discovery and evals, and a self-contained HTML dashboard with evidence bars.
MYREPOS.who: Developers whose AI coding agents keep ignoring or reinventing the house style — and who want proof of what the conventions actually are before enforcing them.
MYREPOS.cost: Free and local-first: zero API keys. The only optional external piece is a local Ollama install, which is also free.
steps: Install the CLI
Clone the repo, then install it as a Python package in editable mode — that gives you the full agent-standards command.

git clone https://github.com/malwar77/agent-standards.git
cd agent-standards
pip install -e .
Or use the zero-dependency shell layer
The shell entrypoint needs no dependencies at all; python3 only upgrades it to exact AST discovery. Set AGENT_STANDARDS_NO_PYTHON=1 to force the pure-shell path.
bin/agent-standards init .
Install the agent command prompts (optional)
Run install.sh inside your own project: it copies the agent command prompts into .agent-standards/commands/, plus .claude/commands/ and .cursor/rules/ where those exist.
./install.sh
Initialise and discover
init creates the .agent-standards/ folder; discover mines convention candidates from your code. Discovery is read-only.

cd your-repo
agent-standards init
agent-standards discover .
Review the candidates
Approve standards interactively, with the evidence shown for every decision — or auto-approve above a confidence threshold.
agent-standards review --auto-approve
Inject, view, enforce, score

inject prints the standards relevant to a task description, ready for your agent. export builds a dashboard; serve runs it live on port 8765; enforce fails (exit 1) on a critical regression; score checks changed code against what was injected.

agent-standards inject "add a retry wrapper for the API client"
agent-standards export . --dashboard
agent-standards serve
agent-standards enforce .
agent-standards score src/foo.py
MYREPOS.watch: The README labels the project EXPERIMENTAL / EDUCATIONAL. Enforcement is opt-in only — nothing is gated until you mark a standard critical: true — and the optional Ollama prose pass is advisory: it cannot alter evidence or approval status.

MYREPOS.name: aetherbot
MYREPOS.blurb: A safety-first crypto trading bot for Python: paper trading by default, risk rules enforced in code, and a local AI that can only say no.
MYREPOS.what: AetherBot is a production-oriented, safety-first open-source crypto trading bot for Python 3.11+, inspired by Freqtrade. It offers CCXT multi-exchange support, dry-run paper trading as the hard default, a local-LLM advisory layer (Ollama — no API keys), Telegram and Web UI control, SQLite persistence, backtesting with benchmark reporting, and an optional scikit-learn ML module. The README is explicit that the software is for educational purposes.
MYREPOS.how: Risk lives in code, never in prompts: every order — paper or live — passes the RiskManager veto (max open trades, stake limits, daily loss halt, max drawdown halt, loss-streak cooldown, stop sanity), and no AI output can bypass it. The Ollama brain annotates every proposal; a verdict of 'against' can skip a signal, but the AI can never create, resize or approve a trade, and hallucinated fields are dropped by construction. The engine only ever acts on the last closed candle, so there is no lookahead bias, and strategies are Python subclasses implementing three populate methods (indicators, entry trend, exit trend).
MYREPOS.who: Python developers who want to study how a trading bot should be engineered — risk gates, paper simulation, backtesting — before ever thinking about live markets.
MYREPOS.cost: The software is free and the AI layer runs locally on Ollama, so there are no API keys. Live trading would put real capital at risk, and the README's warning is blunt: live trading can lead to total loss of capital.
steps: Clone and create a virtual environment
Standard Python isolation so the bot's dependencies never fight your other projects. Needs Python 3.11+.

git clone https://github.com/malwar77/aetherbot.git
cd aetherbot
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
Install the dependencies
Pulls in CCXT, the data and web stacks, and the rest of requirements.txt.
pip install -r requirements.txt
Optional: pull the local AI model
The advisory brain runs on Ollama, fully local — no API keys. Skip this and the bot still trades its strategy rules; it just has no AI annotations.
ollama pull llama3.2
Start it in dry-run (the default)
This is the mandatory first mode: the paper simulator fills every order against real market prices with simulated fees. No real orders are placed.
python -m aetherbot.main start --config config/config.example.yaml
Open the dashboard and use the other commands
The read-only web dashboard runs on port 8080. The CLI also downloads OHLCV history, backtests a pair against buy-and-hold and EMA-cross benchmarks, and scaffolds new strategies.

open http://127.0.0.1:8080
python -m aetherbot.main download-data --days 90
python -m aetherbot.main backtest --pair BTC/USDT
python -m aetherbot.main create-strategy MyStrategy
MYREPOS.watch: The README's safety warnings come first for a reason: this is educational software, nothing in it is financial advice, and live trading can lead to total loss of capital. Live mode is deliberately hard to reach — it requires three fields (dry_run: false, confirmed_live: true, risk_disclosure_accepted: true with a timestamp) set by manually editing the config file; no CLI flag, code path or LLM can set them, and the bot refuses to start live otherwise.

MYREPOS.name: regimedesk
MYREPOS.blurb: A fact-based market regime and technical-analysis desk: deterministic signals, risk vetoes in code, and paper mode unless you opt in by hand.
MYREPOS.what: RegimeDesk is a market regime / technical analysis desk with a trend-following signal core, strict risk management in code, and optional per-user MT5 execution behind an explicit, user-controlled live opt-in. Its signal engine produces proposals — never trades — and every output is labelled facts and proposals only; the README states plainly that nothing in the project is trading advice.
MYREPOS.how: A deterministic regime engine classifies the market, and a trend-following core (TSMOM, moving-average signals, Donchian channels, trend strength, volatility scaling) generates proposals, supported — never triggered — by candlestick patterns, swing structure, support/resistance, and ICT-labelled context (fair value gaps, sessions/killzones, premium/discount), which the README flags as an unverified heuristic framework. Every order, paper or live, passes the RiskManager veto; a per-account kill switch blocks an account whose daily or weekly drawdown limit is breached; and the executor is the only route to any broker, with broker/mode consistency enforced so a paper account can never route to a live broker. Market data comes from OANDA v3 REST, ccxt, or recorded sessions replayed with a no-lookahead guarantee.
MYREPOS.who: Traders and developers who want a disciplined analysis desk — daily technical briefs and logged, explainable signal proposals — with the safety gates engineered in rather than promised.
MYREPOS.cost: The software is free. Live data via OANDA needs an OANDA_API_KEY (a practice account works with OANDA_ENV=practice). Optional MT5 execution trades real money — see the watch-out.
steps: Clone the repo
One command pulls the whole desk onto your machine.

git clone https://github.com/malwar77/regimedesk.git
cd regimedesk
Write today's technical brief
The technical agent analyses the market and writes a dated brief to briefs/technical_YYYYMMDD.md. Read-only — nothing is executed.
python main.py technical
Generate signal proposals

Proposals are generated and logged to the live signal JSONL log — the signal engine never places trades itself. Swap in your own account config from config/accounts/ when you move past the example user.
python main.py signal --user example_user
Check status
A read-only status view for the account: mode, recent proposals, recorded numbers — including losses.
python main.py status --user example_user
Attempt an execution (explicit, gated)

Execution is a separate, deliberate command naming one signal id. It still has to pass the RiskManager veto, the kill switch, and — for live accounts — the manual opt-in and risk-disclosure gates, or it is refused.
python main.py execute --user example_user --signal-id <id>
Run the test suite
The safety model is enforced by tests; run them before trusting any local change.
python -m pytest tests/ -q
MYREPOS.watch: Paper/demo is the hard default: live mode requires the account owner to manually edit their own config (mode: live plus risk_disclosure_accepted: true with a timestamp), and if the disclosure flag is false every live order is refused regardless of any other setting. Connecting a live MT5 account trades real money — the README warns of real financial risk, including loss of the entire balance, and notes that managing trades for other people may require licences in your jurisdiction. ICT-derived features are labelled in code and briefs as an unverified heuristic framework — analysis context, never an auto-trigger.

MYREPOS.name: dexscreener-trading-bot
MYREPOS.blurb: A paper-mode skeleton that scans memecoins on Dexscreener with hard factual filters — and deliberately has no live trading path at all.
MYREPOS.what: This repo (titled 'Memecoin Trading Bot (Dexscreener) — paper-mode skeleton') is a safety-first skeleton for scanning and paper-trading memecoins using Dexscreener's keyless public API. It follows the same contract as AetherBot and RegimeDesk: risk in code, never in prompts; paper mode is the hard default; no invented endpoints.
MYREPOS.how: Three commands do everything. scan pulls pairs from Dexscreener's public search API and applies deterministic, fact-based filters — minimum liquidity, minimum 24h volume, maximum pair age, minimum 24h transaction count — then ranks survivors by 24h volume; no sentiment, no hype heuristics. run loads the paper portfolio, respects paper stops on existing positions, then risk-gates and paper-buys top candidates, with every entry passing the RiskManager veto (max open positions, per-position cap, daily loss halt, invalid-price rejection). status prints honest numbers — cash, marked equity, open positions and total P&L including losses. Fees and slippage are simulated (1% per side by default) and all filters and risk limits are tuned in config/config.example.yaml.
MYREPOS.who: Developers who want to study memecoin market structure and bot safety design with fake money — and anyone who wants to see what a scanner's filters actually keep and reject.
MYREPOS.cost: Free, and keyless: Dexscreener's API is public and needs no API key. The only runtime dependencies are pytest and PyYAML. Paper mode spends nothing.
steps: Clone and install the (tiny) dependencies
The requirements are deliberately minimal — pytest and PyYAML only.

git clone https://github.com/malwar77/dexscreener-trading-bot.git
cd dexscreener-trading-bot
pip install -r requirements.txt
Scan for candidates
Pulls pairs matching the query and applies the factual filters from the config: liquidity, 24h volume, pair age, transaction count. Survivors are ranked by 24h volume.
python -m memebot.main scan --query "SOL/USDC"
Run a paper session
PAPER ONLY: respects stops on existing paper positions, then paper-buys top candidates that pass the RiskManager veto, against the simulated starting balance (default $1,000).
python -m memebot.main run --query "SOL/USDC"
Check the honest status
Cash, marked equity, open positions and total P&L — including losses — with the paper-mode reminder printed.
python -m memebot.main status
Tune the filters

Edit config/config.example.yaml: scanner thresholds (min_liquidity_usd, min_volume24h_usd, max_age_hours, min_txns24h) and risk limits (max_open_positions, max_position_pct, stop_loss_pct, daily_loss_limit_pct).

# config/config.example.yaml
mode:
  dry_run: true            # hard default; leave it
MYREPOS.watch: The README leads with the warning, and so does this guide: memecoins are the highest-risk corner of crypto — total loss of capital is a common, normal outcome, rug pulls and honeypots are routine, and a stop-loss is a mitigation, not a guarantee. By design this skeleton has NO live execution path: the CLI refuses to trade outside paper mode even if you set the live gates in the config, because there is deliberately no live execution adapter. Nothing it prints is financial advice.

MYREPOS.name: ai-trading-stack
MYREPOS.blurb: A curated architecture guide: the 8 open-source repos that make up a serious AI trading stack, organised layer by layer.
MYREPOS.what: ai-trading-stack is not a bot — it is a curated guide: '8 GitHub Repos for Building an AI Trading Stack'. It maps the foundational open-source architecture for autonomous, algorithmic and AI-driven quantitative trading systems, separating a robust system into modular layers so risk bounds stay deterministic, execution stays fast, and AI reasoning stays isolated.
MYREPOS.how: The guide walks six layers, each with its chosen repo. Data & ingestion: CCXT's unified feed across 100+ exchanges. Strategy & alpha: virattt/ai-hedge-fund (specialised LLM agents debating trade theses), FinRL (deep reinforcement learning), Freqtrade/FreqAI and Jesse. Backtesting & validation: NautilusTrader (tick-level deterministic simulation), Jesse, Freqtrade (walk-forward and hyperparameter optimisation). Risk controls: pre-trade checks, drawdown limits, position sizing, kill-switches. Execution: NautilusTrader routing, Hummingbot market making and arbitrage, CCXT direct APIs. Agents & on-chain: ElizaOS as the autonomous agent runtime with wallet interactions. A mermaid architecture diagram in the README shows how the layers connect.
MYREPOS.who: Builders planning an AI trading system who want the map before the code: which proven open-source piece belongs in which layer, and why the layers must stay separate.
MYREPOS.cost: Reading the guide is free. Building from it is not one cost but eight: each curated project has its own requirements — exchange accounts, market-data access, and for the LLM-agent pieces, model API usage.
steps: Read it on GitHub
There is nothing to install — the repo is documentation. Start with the architecture overview and the layer diagram, then read the curated list top to bottom.
https://github.com/malwar77/ai-trading-stack

The README names the three Space secrets the deployment needs: BOT_TOKEN, API_ID and API_HASH. API_ID and API_HASH come from your Telegram account's app credentials at my.telegram.org.

SIGNALS.name: Elevatormusic/hermes-warm-compaction
SIGNALS.blurb: A Hermes Agent plugin that makes context compaction reuse the server's prompt cache instead of re-reading everything — author's benchmark: ~80s down to ~16s.
SIGNALS.what: Hermes Warm Compaction is a context-engine plugin for Nous Research's Hermes Agent. When an agent session compacts its context, the usual approach fires a fresh summary request; this plugin instead re-sends the session's last main-model request plus the new rows and a handoff instruction, so the server reuses its cached prompt prefix and only reads the new rows. It uses only documented plugin APIs — no host patching.
SIGNALS.how: Prompt caching is the whole trick: because the re-sent request shares its prefix with what the server already processed, the cached prefix is cheap and fast, and only the new material costs full attention. The speedup only materialises when the model server actually reuses a prefix cache — hosted APIs with prompt caching, vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, Ollama or LM Studio.
SIGNALS.need: Hermes Agent at commit 45871e10 (2026-10-02) or later, Python 3.10+, and no third-party packages.
SIGNALS.watch: The ~80s → ~16s figures are the author's own benchmark (median 16.8s warm vs 78.5s built-in, synthetic ~105K-token sessions, on a DGX server). The mechanism is credible; the numbers are a vendor benchmark, not independently verified.

bash.note: Three commands, then start a new Hermes session:
bash.code:
hermes plugins install Elevatormusic/hermes-warm-compaction#warm_compaction --enable
hermes config set context.engine warm_compaction

SIGNALS.blurb: Boots Linux on a PS5 via a jailbreak payload and a rest-mode resume trick — real, and bannered EXPERIMENTAL by its own README.

SIGNALS.how: You flash a prebuilt Linux image to a USB drive, run the jailbreak for your firmware from a PC, and send the loader payload to the console. The console enters rest mode; when the orange LED goes static you press power — a white LED means Linux is booting.
SIGNALS.need: A PS5 on firmware 3.00–7.61 or exactly 13.60 (nothing in between, and there is no downgrade), a USB drive of 64 GB or more (external SSD recommended), a USB keyboard/mouse, and a PC to run the exploit chain and send the payload.

# then: enable Rest Mode USB power, disable HDMI Device Link,
# run the jailbreak for your firmware, and send the payload from the PC:

# console enters rest mode → orange LED static → press power → white LED = Linux booting

DAILYPICKS.name: xevrion/hatchzip
DAILYPICKS.blurb: A Rust archive extractor (CLI + desktop app) that extracts huge archives in place — the archive shrinks as your files hatch, so you only need free space for the output.
DAILYPICKS.what: HatchZip is a Rust archive extractor — CLI plus desktop app — that extracts huge archives in place: the archive shrinks as your files hatch, so you only need free space for the output, not output-plus-archive. It handles ZIP, 7z, tar, tar.gz and split archives.
DAILYPICKS.how: It extracts from the end of the archive and truncates each finished part, reusing the freed space for the next files. It computes a space plan before touching anything, refuses if the plan doesn't fit, keeps a 2 GB safety margin by default, and can be stopped, crashed or power-cut mid-run and resumed. Every file's checksum is verified, and hostile archives (path escapes, overlapping entries) are refused up front.
DAILYPICKS.need: Windows 10/11, macOS (Apple Silicon or Intel) or Linux — nothing else for the release binaries. From source: Rust (version pinned in rust-toolchain.toml).
DAILYPICKS.watch: The installers aren't code-signed yet — Windows shows 'Windows protected your PC' (More info, then Run anyway); macOS needs a Privacy & Security allowance. By design it destroys the archive as it extracts, so use --verify-first for downloads you can't get again. 7z archives that are one solid block honestly can't be done in place and are refused with a message saying so.

bash.code:

DAILYPICKS29.name: openclaw/wacli

DAILYPICKS29.what: A scriptable WhatsApp client for the terminal: sync, search and send WhatsApp messages from the command line. DAILYPICKS29.watch: It is not affiliated with WhatsApp or Meta, WhatsApp Web history is best-effort, and sending requires a recipient you are allowed to contact. Do not use it for bulk or spam messaging, which risks the account.

bash.note: From the README (Homebrew). Then pair and search.

brew install openclaw/tap/wacli
wacli auth
wacli messages search "meeting"

DAILYPICKS29.name: jackwener/OpenCLI

DAILYPICKS29.what: A CLI that turns websites and your logged-in browser into deterministic commands for humans and AI agents. A small local daemon plus a Browser Bridge Chrome extension connects OpenCLI to your logged-in Chrome session, so built-in adapters can run site commands without you writing scrapers or handling logins again.
DAILYPICKS29.how: For sites with no adapter, the opencli browser primitives let an agent navigate, click, fill forms, extract and screenshot any page through that same browser session. Commands default to JSON, which is what makes the output usable inside agent workflows.
DAILYPICKS29.need: macOS or Windows for the bundled OpenCLIApp, or Node.js 20.18.1 or newer for the npm route; Google Chrome or Chromium and the Browser Bridge extension; your own logged-in browser sessions for any site that needs login.
DAILYPICKS29.watch: Browser-backed commands act with your logged-in identity, so only run adapters and agent prompts you trust. An agent driving your browser can click, post and change things, not just read.

node --version

DAILYPICKS29.name: ARahim3/DigUp
DAILYPICKS29.blurb: On-device semantic search for your own computer: find files by what is inside them, not by their filenames.
DAILYPICKS29.what: On-device semantic search for your own computer: find files by what is inside them, not by their filenames. You pick folders to index, and DigUp reads the pictures, PDFs, documents, recordings, videos and (optionally) code in them, then embeds everything into one shared vector space in a local SQLite index, alongside a keyword index for exact strings.
DAILYPICKS29.how: A plain-language query then ranks images, PDF pages, audio and video moments and code lines together, and results open at the matching page, timestamp or code line. Nothing you index leaves your computer; it goes online only to download the model once and to check for updates once a day.
DAILYPICKS29.need: An Apple Silicon Mac with macOS 14 or later, or 64-bit Windows 10 or 11, or 64-bit Linux (Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12, Mint 21 or newer); disk space for the one-time 865 MB model download and the local index. No account and no API key.
DAILYPICKS29.watch: The Mac build is the mature one; Windows and Linux builds are marked beta in the README, the Windows installer is unsigned (Windows will warn and you must choose to run it anyway), and a large photo library can take hours for the first indexing pass on a CPU-only machine.

bash.note: Linux, from a downloaded release package — replace x.y.z with the release version. Then open DigUp, let the model download once, pick folders to search, and press the search shortcut in any app.
bash.code: sudo apt install ./DigUp_x.y.z_amd64.deb

win.note: Download DigUp_x.y.z_x64-setup.exe from the repo's beta release and run it (no admin rights needed; replace x.y.z with the release version). The README gives no Windows package-manager install command. The search shortcut on Windows and Linux is Ctrl+Shift+Space.

DAILYPICKS29.name: Panniantong/Agent-Reach
DAILYPICKS29.blurb: One CLI that gives an AI agent eyes on the wider internet, with no paid search API.
DAILYPICKS29.what: One CLI that gives an AI agent eyes on the wider internet: reading and searching Twitter/X, Reddit, YouTube, GitHub, Bilibili, Xiaohongshu and more, with no paid search API. Each platform is an ordered list of backends (a primary tool plus fallbacks), so when one access path breaks, Agent Reach switches to the next tool without changing how the agent calls it.
DAILYPICKS29.how: The agent runs one command per channel and action, such as searching Bilibili or reading a page by URL, and gets clean, structured text back for its context. Login-gated platforms reuse a login you already have on your computer in Agent Reach's own dedicated browser, and the tool itself is read-only: it searches and reads, it does not post, comment, like or send messages.
DAILYPICKS29.need: A desktop computer with a shell-capable AI agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenClaw or similar); uv, which the agent installs if missing; logins on your own machine for login-gated platforms; a Groq or OpenAI key only for speech-to-text on some video and podcast channels.
DAILYPICKS29.watch: Do not install the PyPI package called agent-reach — the README warns explicitly that it is not this project. Also, reading platforms through copied logins and scrapers can breach those platforms' terms and can break or restrict an account, so the README itself recommends using a secondary account for login-gated channels.

bash.note: The README's route is agent-led, not a manual pip install. Tell your agent to install from the install guide, then use the agent's own commands.
bash.code:
agent-reach channels
agent-reach bilibili search "large models"
agent-reach read https://www.v2ex.com/t/123
agent-reach doctor

win.note: The README gives no Windows-only install command. Installation is delegated to your agent via the same install guide above, and the agent installs what the channels need (including uv) on your machine.

termux.note: Can't run in Termux as a supported setup — the README's install flow assumes a desktop agent, uv, and Agent Reach's own dedicated desktop browser, and gives no Termux or Android route.
